extracted.intended_audience: attorneys and practitioners who represent clients in trademark matters before the USPTO (including U.S. counsel for foreign-domiciled applicants); OED respondents and counsel
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedural requirements governing competent, diligent, and honest practice before the USPTO in trademark matters, including signature rules, certification/inquiry obligations, use of TESS, disciplinary violations (competence, diligence, misrepresentation, prejudicial conduct), and sanctions/conditions for suspension and reinstatement.

rubrics_metrics.name: U.S. Counsel Rule (37 C.F.R. § 2.11)
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective August 3, 2019, any foreign-domiciled trademark applicant or registrant must be represented before the USPTO by an attorney who is licensed to practice law in the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Rule was intended to increase compliance with U.S. trademark law and USPTO regulations, improve accuracy of submissions, and safeguard the integrity of the U.S. trademark register (84 Fed. Reg. 31498). Practitioners serving as U.S. counsel for foreign-domiciled clients are expected to know and follow this requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO trademark signature rules (37 C.F.R. §§ 2.193, 11.18)
rubrics_metrics.description: All signatures on trademark documents must be signed by a proper person; trademark documents must be personally signed by the signatory named on the document; an electronic signer must personally enter the signature and place it between two forward slashes ('/').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific citation: 37 C.F.R. §§ 2.193(a), (c), (e); 37 C.F.R. § 11.18(a). Failure to comply with signature rules constitutes improper execution of the submission.

rubrics_metrics.name: TMEP guidance on electronic signatures (TMEP § 611.01(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: All documents must be personally signed. The person(s) identified as the signatory must manually enter the elements of the electronic signature. Another person (e.g., paralegal, legal assistant, or secretary) may not sign the name of a qualified practitioner or other authorized signatory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TMEP emphasizes that typing the electronic signature of another person is not a valid signature; signing the name of another person on paper likewise does not serve as the person's signature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of improper signature
rubrics_metrics.description: If the signature on a trademark application or other submission fails to comply with 37 C.F.R. § 2.193(a) or (e) because it was entered by someone other than the named signatory or not signed by a proper person, the submission is improperly executed and cannot be relied upon to support registration; it normally renders the application void and registration may be invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory and case citations (e.g., In re Yusha Zhang; In re Dermahose Inc.; Ex parte Hipkins; In re Cowan) illustrate consequences and the adverse effect on the integrity of the federal trademark registration process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certifications when presenting papers (37 C.F.R. § 11.18(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner certifies that statements made on their own knowledge are true and that statements made on information and belief are believed to be true; further certifies that, to the best of their knowledge, information and belief, formed after a reasonable inquiry, the paper is not being presented for an improper purpose and legal/factual contentions meet specified standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key subparts (37 C.F.R. § 11.18(b)(2)): (i) not presented for improper purpose (harass/delay/increase cost); (ii) legal contentions are warranted by existing law or nonfrivolous argument for change; (iii) factual allegations have evidentiary support or are likely to have support after reasonable investigation; (iv) denials of factual contentions are warranted or reasonably based on lack of information or belief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable inquiry requirement (37 C.F.R. § 11.18(b)(2)(iii))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner who presents any paper to the USPTO certifies that they have conducted an inquiry reasonable under the circumstances that supports the factual assertions in the paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to conduct a reasonable inquiry (e.g., spending only 3–5 minutes reviewing an application) can support findings of misrepresentation or other violations when the practitioner nevertheless certifies the filing under penalty of perjury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competent representation (37 C.F.R. § 11.101)
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall provide competent representation to a client.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Competence includes appropriate thoroughness and preparation; the Final Order finds violations where filings were reviewed and filed 'with unreasonable rapidity and swiftness' and where practitioner failed to follow U.S. Counsel Rule and 37 C.F.R. § 11.18 requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable diligence (37 C.F.R. § 11.103)
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall act with reasonable diligence in representing a client.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diligence includes devoting sufficient time to client matters, taking reasonable steps to ensure forms comply with the U.S. Counsel Rule, and spending adequate time reviewing applications prior to presentation to the USPTO.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misrepresentation prohibition (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners may not engage in conduct involving misrepresentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include signing declarations attesting to a reasonable inquiry when one was not done, authorizing others to enter the practitioner's signature on filings, and submitting information falsely stating representation of a trademark owner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct prejudicial to USPTO administration (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must not engage in conduct prejudicial to the administration of the USPTO trademark registration system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actions such as improper signing, submitting incorrect ownership information, or other conduct that harms clients' trademark rights or the integrity of the registration system fall within this prohibition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectation to know USPTO materials and TMEP
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners who represent applicants, registrants, or others before the USPTO in trademark matters are reasonably expected to know the relevant laws, rules, regulations, procedures, and provisions of the USPTO Rules of Professional Conduct (and the TMEP).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The agency has published ample, readily available information (e.g., uspto.gov/trademarks; tmep.uspto.gov) and practitioners are expected to consult these resources; ignorance is not an adequate defense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of TESS for clearance/ownership checks
rubrics_metrics.description: The Trademark Electronic Search System (TESS) is a publicly available tool that allows searching the USPTO database of registered trademarks and prior pending applications to find marks that may prevent registration (e.g., likelihood of confusion or prior ownership).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A readily available TESS 'Basic Word Mark Search' can reveal prior registrations (e.g., 'SWAROVSKI') in overlapping product categories; failure to use TESS or to find obvious entries can indicate failure of reasonable inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited recognition & ability to conclude matters (37 C.F.R. § 11.58(f))
rubrics_metrics.description: Respondent may be granted limited recognition for 30 days to conclude work on behalf of clients pending before the Office, with obligations to notify clients if work cannot be concluded in that period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limited recognition is temporary and specific; after the 30-day period, the practitioner is prohibited from using USPTO.gov accounts or filing documents unless reinstated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on USPTO.gov accounts during suspension/reinstatement conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Respondent shall not apply for, obtain, verify, sponsor, or use USPTO.gov accounts for preparing or filing documents with the USPTO until reinstated to practice before the USPTO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: USPTO is authorized to disable or suspend any accounts registered to the respondent; reactivation is respondent's responsibility and may be denied until reinstatement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Client notice obligations upon suspension (37 C.F.R. § 11.58(c)(3)(i))
rubrics_metrics.description: Respondent may satisfy client-notice obligations for foreign-domiciled clients by emailing in the client's native language the requisite 37 C.F.R. § 11.58 notices and a correctly translated copy of the Final Order, to specified email addresses under conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permissible emailing options: (1) to the client's email (if reasonably believed direct access); (2) to an email reasonably believed to be directly accessible to the client; or (3) to the referring foreign-domiciled third person/entity only if respondent takes reasonable measures to ensure forwarding, learns that the client received it, and includes details in the affidavit and any reinstatement petition.

rubrics_metrics.name: List and declaration of improperly-signed filings (21-day obligation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Within 21 days of the Final Order, Respondent must send a letter to USPTO Office of Trademark Examination Policy listing all applications/documents where Respondent is named signatory but did not sign, including document type, filing date, and serial/registration number, accompanied by a declaration/affidavit under 28 U.S.C. § 1746 stating Respondent did not sign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List must include (but not be limited to) the 142 trademark applications signed by foreign entities; the declaration must be signed and compliant with 28 U.S.C. § 1746.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cooperation with USPTO inquiries into improper filings
rubrics_metrics.description: Respondent shall cooperate fully with the USPTO in any present or future inquiry into improper filings by referring foreign-based entities or other associates involved with trademark documents submitted to the USPTO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cooperation is a continuing obligation and a condition of the settlement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probation search/reporting obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: While on probation (including any secondary probation after reinstatement), Respondent must: (i) at least monthly search TESS (or replacing system) for applications identifying her as attorney of record; (ii) promptly inform in writing the USPTO Office of Trademark Examination Policy of each filing identifying her as attorney of record that was made without her knowledge or consent; and (iii) submit quarterly written reports to the OED Director documenting completion of monthly searches and reporting results or correspondence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quarterly reports must state either that no improper filings were identified or provide copies of correspondence sent to the Office of Trademark Examination Policy as described.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedial education and review conditions for reinstatement
rubrics_metrics.description: As a condition of reinstatement, Respondent must provide a declaration that she has successfully completed six (6) hours of continuing legal education credit on ethics/professional responsibility and a declaration that she has thoroughly reviewed all provisions of the TMEP (including signature requirements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Declarations must comply with 28 U.S.C. § 1746 and be submitted to the OED Director as part of any reinstatement petition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order-to-Show-Cause procedure for probation violations
rubrics_metrics.description: If the OED Director reasonably believes Respondent failed to comply with the Final Order or USPTO Rules during probation, the OED Director will issue an Order to Show Cause, send it to the respondent, grant 15 days to respond, and may deliver materials to the USPTO Director requesting immediate additional suspension up to nine months.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The OED Director may also seek discrete discipline based on misconduct forming the basis for the Order to Show Cause; any review sought by Respondent will not postpone the suspension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication and notice of discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: The OED Director shall electronically publish the Final Order in the OED FOIA Reading Room and publish a materially consistent notice of suspension and probation in the Official Gazette.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public posting describes the nature of the misconduct, the terms of suspension/probation, and relevant facts; publication is routine for disciplinary decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Payment of USPTO allowable costs (37 C.F.R. § 11.60)
rubrics_metrics.description: As a condition of probation, Respondent shall pay in full the USPTO's allowable costs incurred in connection with the institution, prosecution, and dismissal of the disciplinary proceeding within sixty (60) days of being informed in writing of such costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Costs are those described in 37 C.F.R. § 11.60 and are required regardless of other conditions.
